name: Carla Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Carla. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Happy to. I'll probably say more than I should, though. My boyfriend Tomás says I always do once someone asks about work.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the housing benefit team at the central benefits office on Harbour Street, and I carry about ninety open cases. Mornings are the post tray and the phone queue: a change of address, a landlord who hasn't been paid, someone whose hours went up so their award has to be recalculated. Afternoons I try to do the hard ones, the eviction notices and the people who've fallen between two systems. What I love is the moment a case clicks and someone gets to stay in their flat. What wears me out is a computer system older than me and the weekly targets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, that sounds like the most likely one to me. Half the things they've promised us at work never turned up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I already say at union meetings: good, now put the money into staff instead of software contracts. We've had a hiring freeze for two years and the phone queue is the proof. Fixing that doesn't need AI, it needs people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved, but not relaxed. The office still has its own problems: the freeze, the backlog, and the talk about merging us with the office across the river. Plateau or not, my manager still gets told to do more with fewer people, and that lands on my desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing and keep putting about two hundred a month into the savings account Tomás and I share. I'd go to more branch meetings, because the merger talk is real whatever AI does. And I wouldn't touch the drafting tool they keep pushing, because it would still be optional.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired, mostly. It's not fear, it's the feeling of running uphill on an ordinary Tuesday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the merger. What would that mean for you day to day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A longer commute, two buses instead of a walk, and a bigger team where nobody knows your cases. I'd still have a job, I'm fairly sure of that. I'm more worried about the claimants who've got used to ringing me directly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the drafting tool. Why not try it, if it's optional?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've read the letters it writes and they're wrong in a confident way. A wrong letter to someone on housing benefit isn't a typo, it's a person who thinks they owe money they don't. I'd rather type it myself and be slow.

say: I'd tell the union branch the money should go into **staff, not software**.
I'd point to the **two-year hiring freeze** as the real reason the phone queue is so long.
think: I'd be **relieved** the hype faded, but the office's own problems wouldn't go anywhere.
The **merger talk** and the backlog would still land on my desk through my manager.
do: Keep saving about **two hundred a month** into the account I share with my boyfriend.
Go to more **branch meetings** to fight the planned office merger.
Keep writing claimant letters myself and **skip the drafting tool**.
feel: **Tired** rather than scared, like running uphill on an ordinary Tuesday.
S0.quote: A wrong letter to someone on housing benefit isn't a typo, it's a person who thinks they owe money they don't.
fieldNote: Her **union instinct** frames everything; she blames the hiring freeze before any technology.
She refuses the drafting tool on **accuracy grounds** and explains it through real claimants.
Even with no real AI change, the **office merger** keeps her uneasy.

steps.text: Save about two hundred a month into the shared account
Attend union branch meetings to oppose the office merger
Keep typing claimant letters herself instead of using the drafting tool

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one I can actually picture. It sounds like the plan they showed us at the all-staff meeting last spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In public I'd say it plainly: if software is deciding housing claims, the public deserves to know who checks it. I'd post that on the union page and say it at my aunt's dinner table. Caseworkers aren't against change, we're against mistakes nobody owns.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, this is the one that gets me. Writing, checking, answering customers, that's my whole job list. The office wouldn't sack me on day one. It would just stop replacing people who retire, and one day the team is six people and a dashboard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the union to get a written agreement on no compulsory redundancies before any rollout, and I'd volunteer for the negotiating group. I'd raise my saving to three hundred a month and cancel the gym and the takeaways. And I'd start looking, quietly, at jobs where you sit with people, like tenancy support at a housing charity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Angry, and a bit ashamed of being angry, because I know I'm slow with this stuff. Under the anger there's a fear of being thirty with no skill anyone wants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're slow with this stuff. If the office offered training on the new tools, would you take it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go if it was compulsory, and I'd sit at the back. I know that's not a great answer. I'd rather spend the time learning tenancy law than learning to supervise a program that's replacing my friends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bev, who eats lunch with me every day, has nineteen years on the team and two years to her pension. If they offered early exits she'd take one, and I'd lose the person who taught me everything. The other is Marcus, who's on a temporary contract and just wouldn't be renewed.

say: I'd say the public deserves to know **who checks** the software deciding housing claims.
I'd post on the **union page** that caseworkers oppose mistakes nobody owns, not change itself.
think: My job list is **writing, checking and answering**, so this picture hits me directly.
The office would **stop replacing** people who retire until the team shrinks to a handful.
do: Join the union **negotiating group** for a no-compulsory-redundancy agreement before rollout.
Raise saving to **three hundred a month** and cancel the gym and takeaways.
Look quietly at **tenancy support** jobs at housing charities.
feel: **Angry**, and a little ashamed of that anger because she knows she's slow with technology.
Afraid of being **thirty with no skill** anyone wants.
S1.quote: The office wouldn't sack me on day one. It would just stop replacing people who retire, and one day the team is six people and a dashboard.
fieldNote: She sees Steady Disruption as the **office's actual plan**, already shown at a staff meeting.
Her first answer to change is **collective protection**, with retraining a distant second.
She admits she'd only take AI training **if compulsory**, an honest gap she owns.

steps.text: Volunteer for the union group negotiating a no-redundancy agreement
Raise monthly saving to three hundred and cancel the gym
Apply for tenancy support jobs at local housing charities

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's before our tenancy even comes up for renewal twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly I'd be the loud one: this needs a law, a pause, and a guaranteed income before anyone switches off a benefits office. I'd march, I'd sign everything, I'd stand outside Parliament in the rain. Somebody has to say that people on benefits shouldn't be processed by a machine nobody voted for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job is gone by 2028, maybe 2029 if the buying process is slow, which it always is. My whole day is thinking work at a desk. The robots coming three years later doesn't help me at all. It only matters for Tomás, who fixes buses with his hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd move every spare penny into savings and cancel the holiday we'd planned for next summer. I'd lean on the union for the biggest severance we can get, and I'd ask my parents if we could move back in with them if it came to it. Then I'd try to get into hands-on support work, like a support worker in a hostel, because a robot that can do that is years further off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. I'd lie awake doing sums on the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your boyfriend's work is hands-on. How would the two of you talk about this at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say we're fine because buses still need mechanics, and for three years he'd be right. I'd say three years is just a delay. We'd probably end up living on his wage while I retrain, which I'd hate, because I've always paid my half.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill goes first if your pay stops?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car, which we barely need anyway, then the streaming and the phone contracts. Rent is the one I'd fight for, because I've seen in my own cases what happens when the rent goes first. I've literally written those letters.

say: I'd demand a **law, a pause** and a guaranteed income before benefits offices close.
I'd **march and sign** everything, saying claimants shouldn't be processed by a machine nobody voted for.
think: My desk job is likely **gone by 2028**, maybe 2029 if buying drags.
The **three-year robot gap** protects my boyfriend's hands-on job, not mine.
do: Cancel next summer's **holiday** and move every spare penny into savings.
Push the union for the **biggest severance** and ask my parents about moving back in.
Retrain toward **hostel support work**, where robots are years further off.
feel: **Sick**, lying awake doing sums on the rent.
S2.quote: My whole day is thinking work at a desk. The robots coming three years later doesn't help me at all.
fieldNote: The **thinking-first, robots-later** order splits her household: her boyfriend's hands-on job buys time.
She'd hate **living on his wage**, a point of pride about always paying her half.
Her casework shows her exactly **what happens** when rent goes unpaid, so rent comes first.

steps.text: Cancel next summer's holiday and put the money into savings
Press the union for the biggest possible severance deal
Ask her parents about moving back in if her pay stops
Train for support worker roles at homeless hostels

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is still fast, but it isn't tomorrow. I'd be thirty-two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as before, only with more time to organise: five years is enough to write the rules properly if the government starts now. I'd push for a public plan for every benefits office, with retraining paid for and nobody finding out from a letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years means I can't pretend I didn't see it coming. The trap for someone like me is that I'd spend three years fighting it and two years panicking. I need to fight it and get out at the same time, and I'm not good at doing two things at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for the two-year evening diploma in social work at the college, starting next autumn. I'd keep my union role and keep saving three hundred a month. By 2030 I'd want to be working with people face to face, where AGI alone can't do the whole job and robots are still years behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a bit of relief in having time, and a bit of dread in having no excuse. Mostly it's a knot in my stomach that doesn't go away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make that course hard to finish?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money and energy. The course is about two thousand a year and I'd be doing it after full days of casework. Tomás would cook more, I suppose, and I'd see my friends less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said you'd rather type letters yourself. Does that change with five years' warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little. I still wouldn't use the tools for claimant letters, but I'd want to know what they get wrong. You can't argue against something you've never looked at, and I've been doing exactly that.

say: I'd say five years is enough to write **proper rules** if the government starts now.
I'd push for a **public plan** for every benefits office, with retraining paid for.
think: Five years takes away my **excuse** for not seeing it coming.
My risk is spending **three years fighting** and two years panicking instead of doing both.
do: Enrol in a **two-year evening diploma** in social work starting next autumn.
Keep my union role and keep saving **three hundred a month** for fees.
Aim to work **face to face** with people by 2030.
feel: **Relief** at having time, mixed with **dread** at having no excuse.
S3.quote: The trap for someone like me is that I'd spend three years fighting it and two years panicking.
fieldNote: With more time she shifts from protest alone to **protest plus retraining**.
She admits a contradiction: she has argued against tools she's **never looked at**.
The diploma costs about **two thousand a year**, paid while working full time.

steps.text: Enrol in the college's two-year evening social work diploma
Stay active in the union and push for paid retraining
Keep saving three hundred a month toward course fees

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven, which is strange to picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift and governments waste gifts. I'd campaign for the boring things: a retraining fund, protected pensions for people near the end, and a rule that nobody gets a benefits decision from a machine without a person they can ring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, with a decade I think I'd be alright myself, but I'd worry for everyone around me. I'd have time to qualify as a social worker and get a few years in. What bothers me is whether social work becomes a screen job too, because a lot of it is already paperwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish this year, then start a part-time social work degree around 2028, so I'm qualified by 2031. We'd keep saving and wait on buying anywhere until we see where the jobs are. And I'd stay in the union the whole time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, but not calm. It's the feeling of having a long to-do list instead of a fire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said governments waste time. Who would you blame if they did?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The ministers who'd rather sign a software contract than fund a team. And the tech firms that sell it as saving money while the mistakes land on the poorest people. I'd vote on it, I know that much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change any plans outside work, like where you live?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd hold off on buying a flat until about 2030. I don't want a mortgage on a salary I'm not sure of. Tomás wants to buy sooner, and that's an argument we already have.

say: I'd say **ten years** is a gift that governments tend to waste.
I'd campaign for a **retraining fund**, protected pensions, and a person to ring about decisions.
think: With a decade I could **qualify** as a social worker and build experience.
I worry social work itself becomes a **screen job**, since much of it is paperwork.
do: Start a **part-time social work degree** around 2028 to qualify by 2031.
Hold off **buying a flat** until about 2030 while saving steadily.
Stay in the **union** throughout and vote on the issue.
feel: **Calmer but not calm**, like a long to-do list rather than a fire.
S4.quote: Ten years is a gift and governments waste gifts.
fieldNote: With ten years she expects to be **alright herself**, and her worry turns outward.
She blames **ministers and tech firms**, consistent with her union politics.
Housing plans already cause **arguments** with her boyfriend, and the timeline sharpens them.

steps.text: Start a part-time social work degree around 2028
Delay buying a flat with her boyfriend until about 2030
Campaign through the union for a public retraining fund
Vote for candidates backing a human contact on benefit decisions

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, without a doubt. Two years isn't enough to retrain, and our savings would last about four months on my side if Tomás's wage didn't cover the rest. What would help is paid retraining while you still have your salary, and a law that a person signs off every benefits decision, so the jobs that are left are real ones.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the claimants. Everyone talks about what happens to people like me, but a machine making mistakes on housing benefit means people losing their homes. Someone should be asking them too.

headlineQuote: A machine making mistakes on housing benefit means people losing their homes.
portrait: Carla is a 27-year-old **housing benefit** caseworker with about ninety open cases and a strong union streak.
She **never uses AI tools**, refusing the drafting tool because its letters are confidently wrong.
In the milder pictures she's worn down by the **hiring freeze** and merger talk, not by technology.
In the fast AGI picture she expects her desk job **gone by 2028** and would lean on her boyfriend's wage.
With more warning she plans **social work training** while campaigning for rules and paid retraining.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years is too short to retrain and her savings last about four months.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining** while she still has her salary.
A law that a **person signs off** every benefits decision.
